aluminum: Aluminium is a light metal used in aircraft, cars, packaging and construction. Producing it takes huge amounts of electricity, so its price also depends on energy costs.
brent: Brent is the world's main benchmark for crude oil, named after a North Sea field. Most of the oil traded globally is priced off Brent.
cattle: Live cattle is a futures contract that tracks the price of beef cattle in the United States. It depends on feed costs, herd size and demand for meat.
cocoa: Cocoa is the raw material for chocolate. Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana grow more than half of the world's crop, so tree diseases and weather there move the price strongly.
coffee: Coffee is one of the most traded agricultural commodities. The benchmark contract is arabica, and prices depend on harvests and weather in Brazil, Vietnam and Colombia.
copper: Copper is the key metal of electrification: wires, electric motors, EVs, power grids and data centres all need it. Its price is often seen as a gauge of the global economy.
corn: Corn (maize) is the world's biggest grain crop by volume: livestock feed, food ingredient and ethanol biofuel. The United States is the top producer.
cotton: Cotton is the main natural fibre for clothing and textiles. The biggest producers are China, India, the United States and Brazil.
eem: iShares MSCI Emerging Markets (EEM) is a BlackRock ETF holding large companies from emerging markets, including China, India and Taiwan.
efa: iShares MSCI EAFE (EFA) invests in large companies from Europe, Australasia and the Far East, excluding the US and Canada.
gasoline: RBOB gasoline is the US futures contract for petrol. Its price depends on crude oil, the summer driving season and how busy refineries are.
gold: Gold is the classic safe-haven asset that has served as a store of value for thousands of years. Central banks, jewellers and investors buy it, especially in times of crisis, inflation or war.
heatoil: Heating oil is a refined oil product used for home heating and closely related to diesel fuel. Its price follows crude oil and winter demand.
hogs: Lean hogs is a futures contract on the price of pork carcasses in the United States. It is driven by feed costs, exports to Asia and animal diseases.
ivv: iShares Core S&P 500 (IVV) is BlackRock's low-cost ETF on the S&P 500 index and one of the largest ETFs in the world.
natgas: Natural gas (US Henry Hub) is a fuel for heating and power plants and a raw material for the chemical industry. Its price is highly seasonal and depends on the weather and LNG exports.
oats: Oats are a grain used for cereal flakes, porridge and animal feed. The futures market is small, so prices can swing sharply on the weather in Canada and the US.
ojuice: Frozen concentrated orange juice is a small futures market. Prices depend on orange harvests in Florida and Brazil, hurricanes and citrus diseases.
palladium: Palladium is a rare platinum-group metal that goes almost entirely into catalytic converters for petrol engines. The main producers are Russia and South Africa.
platinum: Platinum is a rare precious metal mined mostly in South Africa. Its main uses are catalytic converters for cars, jewellery and hydrogen technologies.
qqq: Invesco QQQ is an ETF that tracks the Nasdaq-100, the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on Nasdaq. Tech giants such as Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia and Amazon dominate it.
rice: Rice is the staple food of more than half of humanity. The Chicago exchange trades rough (unhusked) rice; prices depend on Asian harvests and export restrictions.
schd: Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity (SCHD) holds US companies with stable and growing dividends. It is popular with people building passive income.
silver: Silver is both a precious and an industrial metal, used in electronics, solar panels and medicine. Because of that dual demand, its price usually moves more sharply than gold's.
smh: VanEck Semiconductor (SMH) is an ETF holding the biggest chipmakers and chip-equipment companies, such as Nvidia, TSMC, Broadcom and AMD.
soxx: iShares Semiconductor (SOXX) is a BlackRock ETF that invests in US-listed semiconductor companies: chip designers, manufacturers and equipment makers.
soybeans: Soybeans are a major source of plant protein and oil, used for animal feed, soybean oil and tofu. Brazil and the US are the largest producers and China the largest buyer.
soyoil: Soybean oil is one of the world's most widely used cooking oils and also a feedstock for biodiesel, so its price depends on energy policy as well as food demand.
spy: SPDR S&P 500 (SPY), launched in 1993, is the oldest US-listed ETF and tracks the S&P 500 index of 500 leading American companies — often treated as 'the market' itself.
sugar: Sugar is made from sugar cane and sugar beet. Brazil is the largest exporter and turns part of its cane into ethanol, so the sugar price is linked to oil too.
vea: Vanguard FTSE Developed Markets (VEA) invests in companies from developed countries outside the US, mainly Europe, Japan, Canada and Australia.
vig: Vanguard Dividend Appreciation (VIG) invests in US companies that have raised their dividends for at least 10 years in a row.
voo: Vanguard S&P 500 (VOO) tracks the S&P 500 index of 500 large US companies with one of the lowest fees available. It is a popular choice for regular long-term investing.
vt: Vanguard Total World Stock (VT) is a single fund for the whole world's stock market: thousands of companies from the US, Europe, Asia and emerging markets.
vti: Vanguard Total Stock Market (VTI) holds the entire US stock market in one fund — thousands of companies from giants to small caps — at a very low fee.
vwo: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets (VWO) invests in companies from emerging markets such as China, India, Taiwan and Brazil.
vxus: Vanguard Total International Stock (VXUS) invests in companies outside the United States — Europe, Japan, China and other emerging markets — in one low-cost fund.
vym: Vanguard High Dividend Yield (VYM) invests in US companies whose dividend yield is above the market average.
wheat: Wheat is one of the world's staple grains and the raw material for bread and flour. Its price is driven by harvests in the US, Russia, the EU and Ukraine, and by the weather.
wti: WTI is the US benchmark grade of crude oil, priced in New York. Its price moves with OPEC+ decisions, US output, inventories and global demand.
